tagline.text: A quiet island in Quezon, between Lamon Bay and the Pacific Ocean

location.label: Location
location.text: Alabat Island in Lamon Bay, eastern Quezon (municipalities of Alabat, Quezon and Perez)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500~4,000 (per person, 2 days and 1 night from Manila)

children.text: Alabat Island lies in Lamon Bay off eastern Quezon and covers about 192 square kilometers, shared by the three municipalities of Alabat, Quezon and Perez. Still little touched by commercial tourism, it offers a quiet mix of Kabila Beach, waterfall treks, farm visits, and mangrove and mudflat scenery.
Alabat Island sits in Lamon Bay off the east coast of southern Luzon and belongs to the Calabarzon region of Quezon province. It covers about
192km²

and is shared by three municipalities: Perez at the northern tip, Alabat, the largest town, in the middle, and Quezon in the south. The town proper of Alabat is squeezed between Lamon Bay and the Pacific Ocean, which earned it the nickname "Gateway to the Pacific", and a Philippine Daily Inquirer article reportedly called it the "Hidden Paradise of Quezon Province."

The island's nature is quite different from its more popular neighbors. A wide mangrove fringe runs along the southwest shore, and several hundred hectares of mudflats are exposed at low tide. A mountain ridge runs through the interior; from a distance the peaks look like separate islands, and the highest, Mt. Camagong, is known to be around
. The climate is tropical rainforest with no distinct dry season, and rain is heaviest from November to January.

The island's first inhabitants were the Inagta Alabat (Alabat Agta), a Negrito people. Their language is critically endangered, with only about 30 speakers estimated around 2000. A Spanish priest built a small chapel at Gordon in 1882, which laid the foundation of the settlement; later the settlers moved around, and the name Alabat is said to have come into use in the American period. The municipality of Alabat today has about 15,700 residents according to the 2024 census, who live from rice, coconut and calamansi farming and from fishing. The municipalities of Quezon and Perez originally belonged to Alabat and became independent in 1914 and 1929 respectively. The municipality of Alabat consists of 19 barangays and covers about
57.6km²

For travelers, Alabat's appeal is that it is still little known. It is not an island of resort complexes and night markets but a simple trip: you ride a tricycle between fishing villages and mountain roads to reach beaches and waterfalls, see calamansi and cacao on farms, and take a boat to eat lunch at a floating cottage in the middle of Lamon Bay. In return, transport options are few and information on lodging and restaurants is scarce, so plan at least one night and check locally thoroughly. A 2016 report mentioned a nine-seater seaplane from the CCP Complex in Manila to Alabat port in about 20 minutes at ₱4,500 per person, but it is not confirmed whether it still operates, so check current information if you want to use it. There is also a record of a bridge under construction linking the island to Lopez, so access may change in the future. There are also reports that financing has been arranged for a 64 MW wind power project on Alabat.

This beach in Villa Norte has fine sand in some areas and smooth pebbles in others. It opens to the Pacific, so the waves are moody, but the water is known to be clear. Entrance and camping are free, and an open cottage is said to cost about
. The water is described as calm in the morning and the waves as bigger in the late afternoon.
Tumiis Falls is reached from Villa Norte and Bosay Falls around Mt. Camagong, both on foot. Both need a trek, so it is safer to ask a local resident to guide you.
A boat ride of about
15 minutes
takes you to a floating cottage in the middle of the bay where you can have a meal. Lunch over the water is the signature experience of the island.
Giant clams, called taklobo locally, are cultivated here, and snorkeling around the bay is described as possible. The coastal patrol has reportedly shown visitors a large clam.
You can tour coconut, calamansi, cacao and red chili farms and watch how coco sugar is made. Ask the municipality or a local guide in advance about schedules.

Alabat port is known as one of the longest in the province, and with luck you may see giant clams. The quiet streets where residents walk and the fishing village scenery show the mood of the island. The town center consists of Poblacion Barangays 1 to 5, and 14 rural barangays, such as Angeles, Camagong and Villa Norte, are scattered across the island.

In Alabat the Santo Niño Festival is held on the third Sunday of January, the Coconut Festival and founding anniversary on May 15, Flores de Mayo on the last Sunday of May, and the feast of Our Lady of Mt. Carmel (the town fiesta) on July 16. The town comes alive during festivals, but lodging can run short.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night
items.subtitle: From Atimonan port to Kabila Beach

children.text: Take a bus toward Lucena from Manila. The ride from Manila to Lucena is known to take about 4 hours.
Continue from Lucena to Atimonan. It takes about 1 hour by bus, van or jeepney, and the fare is said to be about ₱50~75.
Board the boat to Alabat at Atimonan port. Boats usually leave about every hour, though this varies with weather and waves, and the crossing of Lamon Bay takes about 45 minutes.
Arrive at Alabat port, have lunch in town and check your lodging.
Take a tricycle to Kabila Beach in Villa Norte. It takes about 20 minutes from town and is said to cost about ₱50 per person.
In the late afternoon, when the waves grow bigger, enjoy the sunset and mountain views from the beach and return to the village.
On the second day, pick one of the waterfall trek, the floating cottage in Lamon Bay or a farm visit, finish it in the morning, and return on an afternoon boat to be safe.

items.title: Day two: pick your activity
items.subtitle: Choose among waterfall, sea and farm

children.text: Have breakfast and settle on a local guide. Ask your host about the weather and trail conditions first.
Start the Tumiis Falls trek from Villa Norte. After rain the trail is slippery, so wear sturdy shoes.
If you like, take a boat about 15 minutes out to the floating cottage in Lamon Bay for lunch or snorkeling.
Visit a calamansi or cacao farm, or a place where coco sugar is made. You need to ask in advance.
Return to Alabat port and board the boat to Atimonan. Boats change with the weather, so leave plenty of time.
Do not try to do all three; the knack of an Alabat trip is to pick one or two and enjoy them at a relaxed pace.
The usual way is to take a Bicol-bound bus from Manila and get off at Atimonan port, or to go to Lucena Grand Terminal and transfer to a bus for Atimonan.
The bus from Manila to Lucena takes about
4 hours
and is said to cost about ₱200~250.
From Lucena to Atimonan is about
1 hour
and is said to cost about ₱50~75.
The boat across Lamon Bay from Atimonan to Alabat takes about
45 minutes–1 hour
and is said to cost about ₱90~110.
Boats may be cancelled or rescheduled depending on weather and sea conditions. Check the latest schedule at the port before you set out.
A daily roll-on/roll-off vessel is said to operate, so you can bring a private car.
A public passenger boat from San Andres port is also said to exist, but its schedule is described as irregular. Check the schedule for each port locally.
The main way to get around the island is by tricycle. From Alabat town to Kabila Beach it is said to cost about ₱50 per person.
There are few vehicles and walking is easy, and the island is described as not unsafe, but avoid traveling late at night.

Alabat Island has a tropical rainforest climate with no distinct dry season. For the municipality of Alabat, annual rainfall is about 3,363 mm; the driest month is April (about 84 mm) and the wettest is December (about 722 mm). Average monthly temperatures range from about
in January to about
in May.

Because you have to cross the water by boat, February to April, when the sea is calm and rain is lighter, is the most reliable time. Avoid the typhoon season from June to November if you can, since sea crossings can be dangerous, and always confirm at the port that boats are running.

Lodging is mainly small guesthouses and homestays in Alabat town and coastal villages, and resort facilities are said to be few. Near the beach there are places where you can use a restroom for a small fee. Book ahead during festivals, and the municipality has offered packages that combine transport and lodging, so it is worth asking.

Food centers on rural eateries and stalls in Alabat. The island is known for "hila-hila" chicharon and tikoy, and meals are described as very cheap. There are few shops near the beach, so buy food at the village market beforehand and try the buko juice from the coconut palms along the shore.
Plan at least 2 days and 1 night. One guide says it takes about
10 hours
one way from Manila.
Boats depend on the weather. On your return day, leave plenty of margin for the morning and afternoon boats.
There are few shops near the beach, so buy water and snacks beforehand.
The waterfalls require a trek. Ask a local resident to guide you.
Bring plenty of cash. ATMs and card payments may be hard to find on the island.
Kabila Beach opens to the Pacific and the waves grow in the afternoon, so swim in the morning.
Ask the municipality or a local guide in advance about farm experiences and package tours.
Boats across Lamon Bay are cancelled depending on the weather. Avoid sea crossings in typhoon season and confirm at the port that boats are running.
Kabila Beach opens to the Pacific and the waves grow in the afternoon, so swim in the morning, and be careful in places without lifeguards.
Waterfall and mountain trails are slippery after rain and the route can be unclear, so do not go alone.
Much of the information on lodging, restaurants and transport on the island is outdated, so check locally before you visit.
Do not damage the giant clams (taklobo) or the mangroves.
There is almost no transport at night, so avoid traveling late.
The hub city on the way to Atimonan, where you change buses from Manila toward Alabat Island. A good place to take lunch or stay overnight on the way to Alabat.
A historic town near Lucena that you can stop by on the way to Alabat.
Another island in Quezon that can be combined with Alabat in a Quezon island itinerary.
An island off the western sea of Quezon. It lies in the opposite direction from Alabat, but is a candidate for the same Quezon trip.
